QuoteOpen: In 1995, Sheldon Axler wrote a paper with a fighting title: Down with Determinants!
In it, he says: determinants are difficult, non-intuitive, and often defined without motivation.
Avi Wigderson sees it very differently: the determinant is undoubtedly the most important polynomial function in mathematics.
So which is it? Let's take a look.
Opening: Most of us met the determinant as a formula: a d minus b c.
It tells us whether a system of linear equations has a unique solution.
It measures how much a linear transformation scales area. Here, every area doubles.
And when it's zero, everything gets squashed flat.
It even finds the area of any polygon.
One of the most beautiful and unexpected places I've found determinants is combinatorics.
And today, I want to show you how determinants can count.
Counting is usually brutally hard. But sometimes, one determinant does it.
Let's start with a simple puzzle.
Hook: They both live in a grid-like world.
And they both want to get back home, right now.
On this grid there are rules. An ant can only step up, or to the right. Never down, and never left.
Of course, there are many paths home. The blue ant could go this way, or this way. And the orange ant, this way, or that way.
But today, they can't just take any path. They had a fight, and if they meet, they'll start fighting again.
So neither will set foot on any dot the other one walks on. Not even later: ants leave a scent trail.
So, how many pairs of paths get them home without intersecting?
You can always find one easily. Here, the blue one goes up and around, and the orange one goes right and around. They never meet.
And here's one where they cross.
Let's check them all, one by one. This pair works. This one doesn't. Neither does this one. Or this one. And so on.
Twenty pairs never meet, and sixteen do.
ListRoutes: First, those four numbers. How many ways can ant one get home? Take a guess.
Let's list them. Right, right, up, up. Right, up, right, up. Right, up, up, right. Up, right, right, up. Up, right, up, right. And up, up, right, right.
Notice: every route is four steps, two right and two up. That's forced: home is two columns right and two rows up.
Slots: So a route is just a choice of which two of the four steps go right.
The same works for any start and home: a steps right and b steps up gives a plus b choose a routes.
Ant one to its own home: six. To the other home: four. Ant two to the first home: four. To its own: six. That's our little square.
OneGoodPair: Here's one. Ant one goes up first, ant two goes right first.
They never meet. Peace in our time.
BruteForce: To find them all, the honest way: each ant has six routes, so thirty-six pairs.
Check them one by one. This pair never meets. This one meets. So does this one. And so on.
TableAndDet: I know what you're thinking: this is stupid. There must be an easier way. Well, here comes an old friend.
Consider this two-by-two matrix, A. Its rows are the ants, and its columns are the houses.
The first entry counts the paths from the blue ant to its own home. There are six.
The second entry is a little sneakier: the paths from the blue ant to the orange ant's house. There are four.
And by symmetry, the orange ant gives the same numbers the other way round: four, and six.
Now find the determinant of A: six times six, minus four times four,
ThreeAnts: In fact, there's nothing special about this scenario.
Make the grid bigger, and bring in a third ant, with a house of its own.
Build the same kind of matrix: three ants, three houses, and each entry counts the paths from one ant to one house.
And fifty is exactly the number of ways all three ants can get home without any of their paths intersecting.
WhyCard: Let's get back to our two ants, and work it out.
AllPairs: Here's the thing that bugged me. Six times six counts all thirty-six pairs going home.
Four times four counts the pairs where the ants swap houses: also sixteen.
So for the determinant to give twenty, the minus sign must cancel the sixteen meeting pairs against the sixteen swapped ones.
So they must match up, one to one. Let's see how.
SwappedToMeet: Take a pair where the ants swap houses.
The blue ant starts to the left of the orange one, and ends to its right.
So somewhere, they must share a dot.
Take the first shared dot, and swap the tails from there.
Now each ant is at its own home, and their paths meet.
MeetToSwapped: Now the other way: a pair that meets on the way home.
Swap the tails at the first shared dot, and they end up in each other's houses.
Swap again at the same dot, and we're back where we started.
Bijection: So swapped pairs and meeting pairs match up, one to one.
This meeting pair goes with this swapped pair.
And this one, with this one.
Formula: Six times six counts every pair going home: twenty that never meet, and sixteen that meet.
Four times four counts the sixteen swapped pairs.
They cancel the meeting pairs exactly.
A bijective proof: the only kind a combinatorialist fully trusts.
LemmaCard: So far, ants on a grid. Now, the general lemma.
BookQuote: Martin Aigner and Günter Ziegler begin their chapter on this lemma like this: The essence of mathematics is proving theorems, and so, that is what mathematicians do: they prove theorems.
But to tell the truth, what they really want to prove, once in their lifetime, is a Lemma.
And this is one of those lemmas.
LGVNames: Bernt Lindström found it in 1973, in matroid theory.
Ira Gessel and Xavier Viennot rediscovered it in 1985, and showed how much it can do.
GeneralLemma: Take any one-way network: roads you can only travel in one direction, with no loops.
Pick some starting points, a one up to a n, and the same number of ends, b one up to b n.
Build a matrix M: the entry in row i, column j counts the paths from a i to b j. From a one to b two, there are four.
Then the determinant of M counts the families of paths, a one to b one, all the way to a n to b n, that never touch.
As long as, like on our grid, any crossed pairing is forced to touch. Here, the determinant is thirteen: exactly thirteen families that never touch.
And a determinant is fast: about n cubed steps for an n by n matrix, while checking every family one by one explodes.
MoveHomes: You might be thinking: surely that's a fluke of this little grid. Move the second house around, and each time, brute force and the determinant agree.
As long as the order stays the same: ant one's house up and to the left of ant two's.
Swap the order and there are no peaceful routes at all. The determinant notices: it counts the swapped pairing instead, with a minus sign.
SekiJoins: Add a third ant, with its own start and its own house.
A three-by-three table: fifty. Brute force over all the triples: fifty.
LemmaVisual: Here's the general statement, on our three ants. Take a one-way network with some starts and some ends, and count the paths from each start to each end. That's the matrix.
Expand the determinant. Each term picks an end for every start, a pairing, with a plus or a minus sign, and counts every family of paths for that pairing.
Here: two hundred and sixteen, minus ninety-six, minus ninety-six, minus six, plus sixteen, plus sixteen.
Of the two hundred and sixteen, only fifty never touch. And when the starts and ends are lined up in order, a crossed pairing always touches.

Now the tail swap from before pairs every touching family with one of opposite sign: one hundred ninety-eight against one hundred ninety-eight. Mathematicians call this a sign-reversing involution. They all cancel.
What's left is exactly the fifty families that never touch. And that is true for any such network.
This is the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma. Lindström found it in 1973; Gessel and Viennot rediscovered it in 1985 and showed how much it can do.
Physicists call walkers like ours vicious walkers. Given that our ants had a fight, that seems fair.
Brute force over n ants explodes. A determinant takes about n cubed steps, or n to the omega with fast matrix multiplication.

And omega keeps falling. Strassen broke three in 1969, and last month it reached nine quarters. Proved by an AI model at OpenAI, checked in Lean, and explained to the rest of us by Amir Shpilka. Division of labour, 2026.
PatternCard: So any puzzle that is secretly a family of paths that never touch, a determinant can count.
Does the pattern repeat? Let's look.
Hexagon: Take a hexagon, cut into little triangles.
Glue two neighbours together and you get a tile. Tiles point in three directions.
Now cover the hexagon with tiles: no gaps, no overlaps. Notice anything? It looks like a stack of boxes.
It's completely flat. Your brain is doing the 3D for free.
How many ways can you tile it?
Fade out the flat tiles. The others link up into chains, from left to right.
Tiles never overlap, so the chains never touch.
Now squash the hexagon onto our grid, and the two chains become our two ants.
So there are twenty tilings. All this time, our ants were tiling a hexagon.
WhatLGVCounts: So what can it count? The grid doesn't matter. Any network of one-way roads with no loops: right, up, diagonal, some roads missing.
Count the routes from every start to every end, and take the determinant.
You get the number of ways for everyone to travel without ever meeting. Here it's forty-two. Of course it is.
So any puzzle that is secretly a family of non-touching paths, a determinant can count. And these puzzles are everywhere.
HexTiling: Here's a hexagon with every side of length two, cut into little triangles.
Glue two neighbouring triangles together and you get a tile: a lozenge. Lozenges come in three orientations.
A tiling covers the hexagon exactly with lozenges. Nothing sticking out, nothing overlapping.
Here's one. Notice anything? It looks like a stack of boxes in the corner of a room.
It's completely flat. Your brain is doing the 3D rendering for free.
So how many tilings are there?
TilesToPaths: Here's the trick. Fade out the flat tiles.
Every other tile has two vertical edges. Enter through one, leave through the other, and keep going. Two edges on the left give two chains.
Tiles never overlap, so the chains never touch. And going backwards, any two chains that don't touch fill in to exactly one tiling.
Now squash the hexagon onto our square grid. Each chain becomes a route of two steps right and two steps up, starting and ending exactly where our ants do.
So the number of tilings is twenty. The same twenty. All this time, our ants were tiling a hexagon.
Boxes: Make the box bigger: three by three by three, and stack the boxes in.
Now there are three chains, so three ants.
Squash it onto a grid: three ants that never touch.
Same recipe as before: count the paths from each ant to each house, and take the determinant.
Nine hundred and eighty stacks of boxes.
Percy MacMahon counted these over a century ago, with heavy algebra. Our ants do it with one determinant.
BoxesCorner: Seen in 3D, a tiling is a stack of boxes in a corner, each stack no taller than the ones behind it.
A bigger box, three by three by three, gives a bigger hexagon and three chains: three ants that never meet.
A three-by-three determinant counts them: nine hundred and eighty.
Percy MacMahon found a formula for every box, over a century ago. Combinatorialists call these plane partitions.
Mountains: Here's a mountain range: every step goes up or down, and it never dips below sea level. It starts and ends at sea level.
How many ranges are there? With two steps, just one. With four steps, two. Six steps: five. Eight steps: fourteen.
One, two, five, fourteen: these are the Catalan numbers, one of the most famous sequences in combinatorics.
They count many things. Read each up-step as an opening bracket, and each down-step as a closing one: every range becomes a balanced string of brackets.
They also count the ways to cut a pentagon into triangles: five again.
Now draw two ranges, one inside the other, and they must never touch.
They're paths again: two walkers, starting here and here, ending here and here.
From the blue start to the blue end is four steps: two ranges. To the orange end, six steps: five. The orange walker gets five, and fourteen.
So the matrix is made of Catalan numbers, and its determinant, two times fourteen minus five times five, is three.
And here they are: exactly three.
CatalanMountains: Another disguise. A mountain range: each step goes up or down, and it never dips below sea level.
How many ways can you draw two ranges, one inside the other, without touching?
A single range is counted by the Catalan numbers. Put four of them in a two-by-two table: the determinant is three.
And here they are. Exactly three.
AztecTiles: And one more, a real beauty: the Aztec diamond. Rows of two, four, six squares, and then back down.
Cover it with dominoes. Each domino covers two neighbouring squares.
The smallest diamond can be tiled in two ways.
The next one, in eight ways.
One thousand and twenty-four. Powers of two, every single time. That's suspicious.
AztecPathsD: Here's the trick. Colour the board like a chessboard.
Now every domino is one of four kinds: lying flat or standing up, and starting on a light or a dark square.
Give each kind a job: a flat step, a step up, a step down, or nothing at all.
Put the steps together, and they link up into paths, from the left side to the right side.
Dominoes never overlap, so the paths never touch. And every pair of paths that never touch comes from exactly one tiling.
So, same recipe as before: count the paths from each start to each end.
Two times six, minus two times two: eight. Exactly the eight tilings.
One size up, there are three paths, and a three-by-three determinant gives sixty-four.
In general, the diamond of order n has two to the power n times n plus one over two tilings. A determinant, hiding in a pile of dominoes.
AztecIntro: And one more, a beauty. This is an Aztec diamond: rows of two, four, six squares, and back down.
Tile it with dominoes. The smallest one has two tilings. The next has eight. The next, sixty-four.
One thousand and twenty-four. Powers of two, every time. That's suspicious.
AztecPaths: Colour the board like a chessboard, and there are four kinds of domino. Give each kind a job: a flat step, a step up, a step down, or nothing.
Now the dominoes link up into paths, from the left side to the right. Dominoes never overlap, so the paths never touch, and every such family comes from exactly one tiling.
So once again: count routes, take the determinant. Twelve times two minus four times four. Eight.
In general, order n gives two to the n times n plus one over two. A determinant, hiding in a pile of dominoes.
ArcticCircle: Now pick one tiling at random, every tiling equally likely, on a big diamond, and let it grow.
The corners freeze into brick walls. The middle is chaos. And as the diamond grows, the boundary between them becomes a perfect circle.
It's called the arctic circle theorem.
SignsCard: But not every counting problem is secretly paths. What then?
With the ants, the bad terms cancelled on their own: every pair that met had a swapped partner with the opposite sign.
With dominoes, nothing like that happens by itself. So we'll have to fix the signs ourselves.
Dominoes2x3: Take dominoes on a chessboard. Dominoes aren't paths, but there's a determinant trick here too. Start small: a two-by-three board.
It can be tiled in exactly three ways: three standing dominoes; one standing on the left and two lying flat; or two lying flat and one standing on the right.
Notice: a domino always covers one dark square and one light square, right next to each other.
So build a matrix: one row for each dark square, and one column for each light square.
Put a one wherever a dark and a light square touch, and a zero where they don't.
Now, a three-by-three determinant is a sum of six terms. Each term picks one entry from every row and every column, and multiplies them.
Three of the six terms pick up a zero, so they vanish.
The other three pick only ones. And each of them is exactly a tiling: a picked one is a dark and a light square that touch, which is a domino.
So the determinant should be three. It's minus one.
The culprit is the signs. Each term also gets a sign: plus if its pattern can be sorted with an even number of swaps, minus if it takes an odd number.
This tiling needs two swaps, so it gets a plus. These two need one swap each, so they get a minus.
One, minus one, minus one: minus one. The cancellation eats the good ones.
KastFix: In 1961, the physicist Pieter Kasteleyn had an idea: if the signs don't cancel the way you want, change the signs.
Draw the board as a graph: a dot for each square, and an edge for each pair of squares that touch. Every edge is a place a domino could go.
Now put a minus sign on just this one edge. In the matrix, its one becomes a minus one.
Which tilings notice? Only the ones that use this edge, and only the all-standing tiling does.
Its term was plus one. Now one of its three entries is minus one, so the term becomes minus one. The other two terms never use that edge, so they stay the same.
Now every tiling carries the same sign, so nothing can cancel. The determinant is minus one, minus one, minus one: minus three.
Ignore the sign, and you get three: exactly the number of tilings.
SmallBoard2: Take dominoes on a chessboard. Dominoes aren't paths, but there's a determinant trick here too. Start small: a two-by-three board has three tilings.
A domino joins a black square to a white neighbour. Write a one wherever they touch. Each tiling picks one entry in every row and every column: one term of the determinant.
If determinants count pairings, this should give three. It gives minus one.
The terms come with signs: plus for this one, minus for these two. Here the cancellation eats the good ones.
SignFix2: In 1961 the physicist Pieter Kasteleyn had an idea: if the signs don't cancel the way you want, change the signs.
Put a minus sign on this one edge. Only the all-vertical tiling uses it, so only its sign flips.
Now every tiling carries the same sign. The determinant is minus three. Ignore the sign: three.
Board4x4: Let's try a bigger board: four by four. It has thirty-six tilings.
Build the plain matrix, eight by eight, and take its determinant. It says there are zero tilings. Very confident, very wrong.
Here's what happened: eighteen tilings come with a plus sign, and eighteen with a minus. They cancel perfectly.
So use Kasteleyn's trick: put minus signs on the vertical edges of every other column.
Now all thirty-six tilings get the same sign, and the determinant gives thirty-six. Exactly right.
KastWhy: Why does every other column work? Look at any little square of four edges. It always has exactly one minus sign: an odd number.
That's Kasteleyn's rule: if every little square has an odd number of minus signs, then every tiling gets the same sign. Let's see why.
Take two tilings, and lay one on top of the other.
Where they agree, nothing happens. Where they differ, their dominoes join up into closed loops. Here, there are two.
To go from one tiling to the other, you turn each loop: every domino on it slides over by one.
The small loop first. Two flat dominoes become two standing ones. That's one swap, so the sign flips once.
But the standing pair uses exactly one minus edge, so it flips once more. Two flips: no change.
Now the big loop. Turning it takes three swaps: three flips. And it picks up one minus edge: a fourth flip. Again, no change.
Kasteleyn showed that this always happens: if every little square has an odd number of minus signs, every loop flips the sign an even number of times.
So any two tilings have the same sign. Nothing cancels, and the determinant counts every single tiling.
FKT: Now the full chessboard, with the same signs: minus on the vertical edges of every other column. The determinant is twelve million, nine hundred eighty-eight thousand, eight hundred sixteen.
Listing one tiling per second would take five months. The determinant does it in an instant.
And it's not really about chessboards. Squares are vertices, dominoes are edges, and a tiling is a perfect matching.
By 1967, Kasteleyn had made it work for any graph you can draw without crossings. This is the FKT algorithm: it counts the perfect matchings of any planar graph, in polynomial time.
And the story kept going. In 1989, Vijay Vazirani pushed it to graphs with no K three three hiding inside, and Leslie Valiant later built his holographic algorithms on top of it.
When a physicist needs to count twelve million tilings, they don't count. They take a determinant, and then let the board go to infinity.
Map: Let's step back. Ants that never meet. Tilings of a hexagon. Boxes in a corner. Mountain ranges. Aztec diamonds. Chessboards.
All counted by one determinant each.
Finale: And it's the same trick every time. Count everything, the families that meet and the ones that don't, each with a sign.
The meeting ones pair up with opposite signs, and cancel. What's left is exactly what you wanted.
For a computer scientist, that's remarkable. Counting is usually hopeless: counting perfect matchings of a general graph is sharp-P complete. That's Valiant, in 1979.
But if your puzzle turns into non-touching paths, or a matching on a planar graph, it becomes one determinant, and polynomial time.

And this isn't only a trick for puzzles. In 1997, Meena Mahajan and V. Vinay computed the determinant itself the same way: write it as a big signed sum, pair up every unwanted term with one of opposite sign, and let them cancel. No division needed.
Determinants can count, because minus signs can cancel.
Goodbye: As for our ants: they can finally go home in peace. Twenty ways home, and they never had to meet.
ReadCounts: Here's the thing that bugged me when I first saw this. Six times six counts every way to send each ant to its own home, including the pairs that meet.
That's the twenty that never meet, plus the sixteen that do.
Four times four counts something stranger: each ant walking to the other one's house.
So the determinant is: never meet, plus meet, minus swapped. For that to equal twenty, the swapped pairs must cancel the meeting pairs exactly. Not roughly. Exactly. Let's match them up.
SwapPaths: Walk along the blue ant's path, and stop at the first dot the orange ant also visits.
From that dot on, swap their tails. The blue ant keeps its start but takes the orange ant's ending, and the orange ant does the opposite.
Look where they end up: each at the other's house. A meeting pair became a swapped pair.
SwapTwice: Nothing before that dot changed, so it's still the first meeting point, and swapping there again puts everything back.
Do it twice and nothing happened. Mathematicians call that an involution. Like most committee meetings.
So meeting pairs and swapped pairs come in perfect couples.
DiagonalSweep: One worry left: could a swapped pair avoid meeting, and have no partner?
Sweep a diagonal across the grid. Every step moves an ant onto the next diagonal, so on each diagonal, each ant stands on exactly one dot.
Track the gap between their columns. At the start, the blue ant is one column to the left.
At the end, it's one column to the right.
And from one diagonal to the next, the gap changes by at most one.
So somewhere it is zero: they share a dot. That's the intermediate value theorem, in its most humble form.
PutTogether: So every meeting pair has exactly one swapped partner, and every swapped pair has exactly one meeting partner.
In the determinant, they cancel. The minus sign isn't throwing things away at random: it removes an exact copy of the meeting pairs.
What survives is exactly the twenty pairs that never meet.
A bijective proof: the only kind a combinatorialist fully trusts.
